title: The nervous system: structure and function

notes.definition: The nervous system enables humans to react to their surroundings and to coordinate their behaviour, by carrying information as electrical impulses along neurones between receptors, the central nervous system and effectors.
explanation: Information from receptors passes along cells called neurones as electrical impulses to the central nervous system (CNS). The CNS is the brain and spinal cord. The CNS coordinates the response of effectors, which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones. The general pathway is: stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response.

Neurones are adapted to carry impulses quickly over long distances. They have a long axon to carry the impulse, branched endings (dendrites and nerve endings) to connect with many other cells, and many axons are covered by a fatty myelin sheath that insulates them and speeds up the impulse. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS, relay neurones carry impulses within the CNS, and motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors.

Neurones do not touch each other. The junction between two neurones is called a synapse. When an electrical impulse reaches the end of a neurone, a chemical is released. It diffuses across the gap and binds to receptors on the next neurone, which starts a new electrical impulse. Because the chemical is only released from one side, impulses cross a synapse in one direction only.

Reflex actions are automatic and rapid. They do not involve the conscious part of the brain, so no time is spent thinking about the response. Reflexes protect the body from harm, for example pulling your hand away from a hot object or blinking when something comes towards your eye.

In a reflex arc, a receptor detects the stimulus and sends impulses along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord (or an unconscious part of the brain). A synapse passes the impulse to a relay neurone, and another synapse passes it to a motor neurone, which carries the impulse to the effector. The effector, such as a muscle, produces the response.

Reaction time is the time taken to respond to a stimulus. It can be measured with a ruler-drop test or a computer test. Factors such as caffeine, practice, tiredness or distraction can change it. When analysing data, repeat readings, calculate a mean, ignore anomalous results and plot data on graphs or bar charts as appropriate.
keyFacts: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord.
Neurones carry information as electrical impulses.
Effectors are muscles (which contract) or glands (which secrete hormones).
Pathway: stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response.
Sensory neurones: receptor to CNS. Relay neurones: within the CNS. Motor neurones: CNS to effector.
A synapse is a gap between neurones; a chemical diffuses across it to start an impulse in the next neurone.
Reflex actions are automatic and rapid and do not involve the conscious part of the brain.
Reflex arc: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector.
Required practical: investigate the effect of a factor on human reaction time.
Long axons, branched endings and a myelin sheath adapt neurones to carry impulses quickly.

keyTerms.definition: A nerve cell that carries electrical impulses.
The brain and spinal cord, which coordinate responses.
A neurone that carries impulses from a receptor to the CNS.
A neurone in the CNS that carries impulses from a sensory neurone to a motor neurone.
A neurone that carries impulses from the CNS to an effector.
The junction (gap) between two neurones, across which a chemical diffuses to pass on the signal.

The time between a stimulus and the response to it.

workedExamples.title: Calculating a mean reaction time with an anomaly
workedExamples.question: A student measured their reaction time five times: 0.24 s, 0.26 s, 0.25 s, 0.48 s and 0.23 s. Calculate the mean reaction time.
steps: Look for anomalies: 0.48 s is roughly double the others, so it is anomalous (perhaps the student was distracted). Leave it out.
Divide by the number of values used: 0.98 ÷ 4 = 0.245 s.

workedExamples.title: Percentage change in reaction time
workedExamples.question: Before drinking a caffeinated drink a student's mean reaction time was 0.30 s. Afterwards it was 0.24 s. Calculate the percentage decrease.

workedExamples.title: Converting a ruler-drop distance to a time
workedExamples.question: In a ruler-drop test the ruler fell 0.20 m before it was caught. Use the equation time = √(2 × distance ÷ 9.8) to calculate the reaction time.
steps: Make sure distance is in metres: 0.20 m (20 cm = 0.20 m).
workedExamples.answer: Reaction time ≈ 0.20 s. (In the exam you will usually be given this equation or a conversion table.)

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the electrical impulse jumps across the synapse.
misconceptions.right: In fact a chemical is released, diffuses across the gap and triggers a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all reflexes go through the brain to be thought about.
misconceptions.right: In fact reflexes do not involve the conscious part of the brain. Many pass through the spinal cord only, which is why they are so fast.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think nerves carry messages, or that "the brain tells the muscle what to do" using messages.
misconceptions.right: In fact neurones carry electrical impulses. Use the word "impulse" in the exam, not "message" or "signal".

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the relay neurone is found in the arm or leg.
misconceptions.right: In fact relay neurones are in the CNS (spinal cord or brain) and connect sensory and motor neurones.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a shorter distance on the ruler-drop test means a slower reaction.
misconceptions.right: In fact a shorter distance means the ruler was caught sooner, so the reaction time is shorter (faster).

realWorld: Doctors tap below the knee to test the knee-jerk reflex, which checks that the spinal cord and nerves in the leg are working.
Drivers' reaction times are slowed by alcohol, drugs and tiredness, which increases stopping distance and the risk of crashes.
Sprinters who leave the blocks less than 0.1 s after the starting signal are disqualified, because such a fast start is treated as anticipating the gun rather than reacting to it.
Many painkillers and anaesthetics work by affecting how impulses pass along neurones or across synapses.
examTips: Always use "electrical impulses", and say they travel along neurones. Do not write "messages".
For a reflex arc, give every step in order: stimulus, receptor, sensory neurone, (synapse), relay neurone, (synapse), motor neurone, effector, response.
At a synapse, say a chemical is released and diffuses across the gap. Electricity does not cross the gap.
In the reaction time practical, name control variables precisely: same hand, same ruler, same starting position of fingers, same person dropping, no warning given.
When calculating a mean, remove clearly anomalous results first and say why.
Reaction time questions often ask you to explain why repeats are taken: to identify anomalies and calculate a more accurate mean.
summary: The nervous system lets us react to surroundings and coordinate behaviour.
Receptors send electrical impulses along neurones to the CNS (brain and spinal cord), which coordinates effectors.
Sensory, relay and motor neurones are linked by synapses, where a chemical diffuses across the gap.
Reflexes are automatic and rapid because they do not involve the conscious brain.
Reaction time can be measured with a ruler-drop test; repeat, remove anomalies and calculate a mean.

options: Sensory neurone
Relay neurone
Motor neurone
Effector neurone
markScheme: 1 mark: sensory neurone
questions.explanation: Neurone A carries impulses from the receptor in the skin to the spinal cord (CNS), so it is a sensory neurone. B is a relay neurone inside the CNS and C is a motor neurone that carries impulses to the muscle (the effector). There is no such thing as an "effector neurone".

questions.question: Which phrase describes a reflex action?
options: Slow and deliberate
Learned and conscious
Automatic and rapid
Controlled by hormones
markScheme: 1 mark: automatic and rapid
questions.explanation: Reflex actions are automatic and rapid and do not involve the conscious part of the brain. Hormonal responses are slower.

questions.question: What is a synapse?
options: The fatty layer around an axon
The junction (gap) between two neurones
The cell body of a relay neurone
The part of the brain that controls reflexes
markScheme: 1 mark: the gap between two neurones
questions.explanation: A synapse is the junction between two neurones. The fatty layer is the myelin sheath.

questions.question: How is the signal passed across a synapse?
options: The electrical impulse jumps across the gap
A hormone is carried across in the blood
The two neurones touch and the impulse passes directly
A chemical diffuses across the gap
markScheme: 1 mark: a chemical diffuses across the gap
questions.explanation: A chemical is released from the first neurone, diffuses across the gap and binds to receptors on the next neurone. Electricity does not jump across, and the neurones do not touch.

questions.question: Which shows the correct order of structures in a reflex arc?
options: Receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector
Receptor → motor neurone → relay neurone → sensory neurone → effector
Effector → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → receptor
Receptor → relay neurone → sensory neurone → motor neurone → effector
markScheme: 1 mark: receptor → sensory → relay → motor → effector
questions.explanation: The impulse starts at the receptor, travels into the CNS along the sensory neurone, passes to the relay neurone and leaves along the motor neurone to the effector.

questions.question:
A student investigates the effect of caffeine on reaction time using a ruler-drop test.
What is the dependent variable in this investigation?
options: Whether or not caffeine was drunk
The length of the ruler
The distance the ruler falls before being caught
The hand used to catch the ruler
markScheme: 1 mark: the distance the ruler falls (which gives the reaction time)
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured: the distance fallen, which is converted to reaction time. Caffeine is the independent variable, and the ruler and hand used are control variables.

questions.question: Why is a reflex action faster than a response that involves thinking?
options: Impulses in reflexes travel along hormones instead of neurones
The impulse does not pass through the conscious part of the brain, so no time is spent deciding
Reflex arcs contain no synapses at all
Motor neurones in reflexes are shorter than sensory neurones
markScheme: 1 mark: does not involve the conscious part of the brain
questions.explanation: In a reflex the pathway avoids the conscious brain, so there is no decision-making delay. Reflex arcs still contain synapses, and hormones are not involved.

questions.question: Where in the body are relay neurones found?
options: In the skin
In muscles
In glands
In the central nervous system
markScheme: 1 mark: in the CNS
questions.explanation: Relay neurones are found in the brain and spinal cord, where they connect sensory neurones to motor neurones.

questions.question:
Impulses can only cross a synapse in one direction.
Which statement explains why?
options: The chemical is only released by the first neurone, and receptors for it are only on the next neurone
The gap is wider on one side
Electrical impulses can only travel towards the brain
The myelin sheath blocks impulses travelling backwards
markScheme: 1 mark: chemical released from one side only / receptors only on the next neurone
questions.explanation: Only the end of the first neurone releases the chemical, and only the next neurone has receptors that it binds to. So the signal can only pass one way.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a reflex action?
options: Catching a ball thrown to you in a game
Writing your name
Pulling your hand away from a hot plate
Choosing what to eat for lunch
markScheme: 1 mark: pulling your hand away from a hot plate
questions.explanation: Withdrawing from a hot object is automatic and rapid and protects you. The other actions involve conscious decisions.

Table 1 shows a student's mean reaction time before and after drinking a cola drink containing caffeine.
Calculate the percentage decrease in the student's mean reaction time.
questions.explanation: Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100 = 0.06 ÷ 0.32 × 100 = 18.75%. Always divide by the original (before) value.

questions.question:
An electrical impulse travels 1.2 m along a motor neurone in 0.010 s.
Calculate the speed of the impulse.
Use the equation:
speed = distance ÷ time
markScheme: 1 mark: 120 m/s
questions.explanation: Speed = 1.2 ÷ 0.010 = 120 m/s. Myelinated neurones carry impulses at high speeds like this, which is why nervous responses are fast.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows a student's reaction times.
One of the results is anomalous.
Identify the anomalous result.
Calculate the mean reaction time without the anomalous result.
markScheme: 1 mark: identifies 0.45 s as anomalous
1 mark: 0.215 s (accept 0.22 s)
questions.explanation: 0.45 s is about double the other values, so it is excluded. Mean = 0.86 ÷ 4 = 0.215 s. Including the anomaly would give 0.262 s, which does not represent the student's typical reaction time.

questions.question:
A sensory neurone from the toe to the spinal cord is 0.90 m long.
Impulses travel along the neurone at 60 m/s.
Calculate the time taken for an impulse to travel along this neurone.
Give your answer in milliseconds (ms).
markScheme: 1 mark: time = distance ÷ speed = 0.90 ÷ 60 = 0.015 s
questions.explanation: Rearrange speed = distance ÷ time to give time = distance ÷ speed = 0.90 ÷ 60 = 0.015 s. Multiply by 1000 to convert seconds to milliseconds: 15 ms.

questions.question: Name the two parts of the central nervous system.
markScheme: 1 mark: brain and spinal cord (both needed)
questions.explanation: The CNS is made up of the brain and the spinal cord.

questions.question:
Muscles and glands are effectors.
Describe how a muscle and a gland each respond to a nerve impulse.
markScheme: 1 mark: muscles contract
1 mark: glands secrete (release) hormones / chemicals
questions.explanation: The CNS coordinates the response of effectors: muscles contract and glands secrete hormones.

questions.explanation: The impulse is electrical in the neurone, but chemical across the synapse. The chemical triggers a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.

questions.question: Explain why reflex actions are important for survival.
markScheme: 1 mark: they are rapid / automatic (no conscious thought)
1 mark: so they protect the body from harm / danger, for example from burns
questions.explanation: Because they are automatic and rapid, reflexes reduce damage, for example by pulling a hand away from heat before it is badly burned.

questions.explanation: The distance the ruler falls depends on how long the person takes to react, so it can be converted into a reaction time.

questions.question: A student investigates whether caffeine affects reaction time. Give two variables they should control.
markScheme: 1 mark each, max 2: same hand used; same ruler; same starting position of the ruler / fingers; same person dropping the ruler; same volume of drink; same time after drinking; same person tested
questions.explanation: Control variables are kept the same so that only caffeine affects reaction time. They must be specific, for example "same hand" not just "same conditions".

questions.question:
In a ruler-drop test, the person dropping the ruler should wait a different length of time before each drop.
Suggest why.
markScheme: 1 mark: so the person catching cannot predict / anticipate when it will be dropped
1 mark: so the result measures a true reaction to the stimulus / is valid
questions.explanation: If the drop came after the same delay each time, the catcher could learn when to close their fingers, giving a time shorter than their real reaction time.

questions.question:
A person's spinal cord is badly damaged in the lower back.
The person can no longer move their legs, even though their leg muscles are not damaged.
Suggest why.
acceptedAnswers: impulses from brain cannot reach motor neurones
markScheme: 1 mark: impulses from the brain cannot pass down the spinal cord (past the damage)
1 mark: so motor neurones do not carry impulses to the leg muscles / effectors are not stimulated
questions.explanation: The spinal cord carries impulses between the brain and the body. Below the damage, motor neurones receive no impulses, so the muscles do not contract.

questions.question:
A person touches a hot pan and quickly pulls their hand away.
Describe the pathway taken by nerve impulses in this reflex action.
markScheme: Indicative content: stimulus is heat (from the pan); receptors (pain or temperature receptors) in the skin detect the stimulus; electrical impulses travel along a sensory neurone; to the spinal cord (CNS); impulse passes across a synapse by a chemical diffusing; to a relay neurone; across another synapse to a motor neurone; impulse travels along the motor neurone to the effector; effector is a muscle (in the arm), which contracts; hand is pulled away; the conscious part of the brain is not involved, so it is rapid and automatic.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear sequence from receptor to effector including sensory, relay and motor neurones in the correct order, with at least one reference to synapses or the spinal cord.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct parts named but the sequence is incomplete or partly wrong.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Strong answers follow the impulse step by step and name each neurone, the synapses and the effector (muscle contracts).

questions.question: Plan an investigation to find out whether drinking caffeine affects human reaction time. Use the ruler-drop test in your plan.
markScheme: Indicative content: independent variable is caffeine (for example drink with caffeine versus the same drink without caffeine); dependent variable is distance ruler falls / reaction time; method: person sits with forearm on table edge, thumb and finger apart; partner holds ruler with zero level with top of thumb; drops without warning, after varying delays; read distance at top of thumb; convert to reaction time using a conversion table; repeat at least 5 times (or more) and calculate a mean, excluding anomalies; then person drinks caffeinated drink, waits a fixed time (for example 10 minutes) and repeats test; control variables: same person tested, same hand, same ruler, same dropper, same volume of drink, same time of day, no practice effect (practise first or test different people); compare means; safety: check no medical condition and that the participant agrees, use a moderate amount of caffeine; improvement: test several people for reliable results.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, detailed method that could be followed to give valid results, with independent, dependent and several specific control variables, repeats and means, and how the reaction time is found.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with most key steps and some control variables, but lacking some detail or logic.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about dropping a ruler and drinking caffeine with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A top-level plan says exactly what is changed, measured and controlled, how many repeats are done and how the results are processed. Mentioning that practice can also improve reaction time, and how to deal with it, shows high-level thinking.
